title.en: Grassroots Democracy – Part 3: Local Government in Urban Areas

text.en: Anita lives in a city, her friend lives in a village. Anita says the city is busy and crowded and people often do not even know their neighbours. But when a building collapsed nearby, dozens of people gathered from all over to clear the rubble and help. The friend says village government is simpler because everyone knows each other. Anita realises that in the city, too, everyone's voice matters. In this chapter we study how towns and cities are governed.

Democracy does not end with voting. In participatory democracy citizens take part in the running of their own area, and local bodies are decentralised, which means local communities have a direct say instead of everything being decided by a central authority. In Chapter 11 we explored the rural, left side of the governance pyramid. Now we look at the urban, right side. Cities and towns are divided into smaller units called wards. Ward committees organise health camps, campaigns against single-use plastics and similar activities. How wards work differs from State to State according to their rules.
The kind of urban body depends mostly on the size of the population. Large cities of more than 10 lakh people have a Municipal Corporation at the top. Chennai and Indore are examples. Towns of between 1 and 10 lakh people have a Municipal Council, also called a Nagar Palika. Smaller towns changing from rural to urban have a Nagar Panchayat. Members of these bodies, called councillors or corporators, are elected by the voters of each ward. The head of a Municipal Corporation is the Mayor. The Municipal Corporation of Greater Mumbai was created in 1865. The Madras Corporation, now the Greater Chennai Corporation, was established on 29 September 1688 and is the oldest municipal institution in India. A Parliamentary Act of 1792 gave it power to levy municipal taxes, which is when municipal administration properly began.
They provide drinking water, drains, sewage disposal, street lights, roads, waste collection, public health, markets, parks and primary schools. They raise money through local taxes, and also receive funds from the State and Central governments. If a water pipe leaks and a lot of water is wasted, citizens can report it to their ward councillor or the municipal office.
For these bodies to work well, people must also do their duties: pay taxes, keep the area clean, avoid littering and wasting water, and look after common property. A group of children who notice a low-hanging electricity wire can warn the authorities. The idea in the city is the same as in the village: everyone's voice matters and everyone should take part.

problem.en: Which urban body would govern a city of 25 lakh people and a town of 3 lakh people?

text.en: More than 10 lakh people: Municipal Corporation.
So the city has a Municipal Corporation and the town a Municipal Council.

prompt.en: How does an urban local body serve citizens and how can citizens help it?

requiredIdeas.en: It provides water, drains, roads, waste collection and health services.
Citizens pay taxes and keep areas clean.
Ward committees give people a direct say.

commonMisconceptions.en: Thinking only the Mayor works for the city.

points.en: Urban local bodies are decentralised and include ward committees.
Municipal Corporation, Municipal Council and Nagar Panchayat depend on population.
They provide basic services and collect local taxes.
Citizens must also perform their duties.
